reference.source: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology / ESE-ENSAT Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Adrenal Incidentalomas
clinicalPearls: An uncommon adrenal lesion, usually found incidentally, classified pathologically as endothelial (lymphangiomatous or vascular), pseudocyst, epithelial, or parasitic
Most are asymptomatic, but large cysts can cause flank or abdominal pain or a palpable mass
Pseudocysts often follow previous adrenal haemorrhage and lack a true epithelial lining
Imaging typically shows a well-defined, fluid-density, non-enhancing lesion, and wall calcification is common
Complex features such as thick walls, septations, soft-tissue components or enhancement raise concern for cystic malignancy or, in endemic areas, hydatid disease
Hormonal evaluation remains appropriate as part of the incidentaloma workup, even though most cysts are non-functioning
Simple asymptomatic cysts are observed, whereas large, symptomatic or complex cysts may require aspiration or excision
reference.pathophysiology: Adrenal cysts arise by several mechanisms. Endothelial cysts result from dilatation of lymphatic or vascular channels; pseudocysts follow organisation and liquefaction of prior haemorrhage or infarction and have no epithelial lining; epithelial cysts derive from glandular or embryonic remnants; and parasitic cysts arise chiefly from Echinococcus. Enlargement produces mass effect, while a haemorrhagic origin explains the frequent finding of a calcified wall.
additionalDifferentials: Cystic adrenocortical neoplasm, benign or malignant
Exophytic renal or hepatic cyst mimicking an adrenal cyst
additionalInvestigations: CT or MRI to confirm fluid density and assess wall thickness, septations and enhancement
Hormonal screening with dexamethasone suppression, metanephrines and aldosterone-to-renin ratio as for any incidentaloma
Serology for Echinococcus where hydatid disease is possible
Cyst aspiration and fluid analysis in selected complex cases
Surgical referral for large or complex or suspicious cysts
redFlags: Complex features such as a thick or enhancing wall, septa or a soft-tissue nodule suggesting malignancy
A suspected phaeochromocytoma presenting as a cystic mass
A possible hydatid cyst where percutaneous intervention risks spillage
reference.prognosis: Very good for simple, non-functioning cysts, which are benign and stable; the outcome depends on excluding the minority that are complex, malignant or parasitic.
pitfalls: Aspirating a cystic phaeochromocytoma without prior biochemical exclusion
Percutaneous puncture of an unrecognised hydatid cyst causing spillage and anaphylaxis
Assuming all cystic adrenal lesions are benign and missing a cystic malignancy
Skipping hormonal screening in an adrenal cyst
references: ESE-ENSAT Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Adrenal Incidentalomas
management: Manage simple, non-functioning, imaging-typical cysts conservatively without intervention
Perform incidentaloma hormonal screening with dexamethasone suppression, metanephrines and aldosterone-to-renin ratio
Characterise the lesion with CT or MRI, assessing wall thickness, septations and enhancement
Treat parasitic (hydatid) cysts with antihelminthic therapy such as albendazole and surgery where appropriate, guided by Echinococcus serology
Undertake interval imaging for indeterminate lesions and consider aspiration with fluid analysis in selected complex cases
Refer for surgical excision of large, symptomatic, complex or suspicious cysts
